Incorporating the Beige Book alongside the June 2022 FOMC decision, the stance remains hawkish (75 bp hike to 1.5–1.75% and balance-sheet runoff) given elevated inflation and persistent supply–demand imbalances. Beige Book reports point to robust job gains, tight labor markets, and widespread wage increases, with many firms passing through higher input and fuel costs, while Russia’s invasion and China’s COVID-related lockdowns are adding to price pressures and supply chain disruptions. That keeps inflation risks front and center even as overall activity has improved modestly from early-year softness.

Balancing this, SLOOS indicates banks generally eased standards for C&I and multifamily loans, kept most other CRE standards steady, trimmed some credit line costs, and saw stronger loan demand for inventories, A/R, plant and equipment, HELOCs, and autos (with RRE mortgages weaker). Foreign banks’ tighter C&I standards flag some cross-border caution, but domestic credit supply and demand look relatively resilient.

Net take: conditions are still cautious because of inflation and policy tightening, but better-than-feared credit dynamics and firm labor markets make the outlook less negative than prior assessments.
